blocks.text: A 13C NMR spectrum is simpler than a 1H spectrum: each peak corresponds to one different environment (type) of carbon atom, and its chemical shift tells which environment. The number of peaks equals the number of different carbon environments. Ethane gives one peak, because both carbons are in the same environment. Propane, CH3-CH2-CH3, has two environments, the two equivalent terminal CH3 carbons and the middle CH2 carbon, so it gives two peaks. Ethanol, CH3-CH2-OH, also gives two peaks: by Table 30.3 the peak at 18 ppm is the CH3 carbon and the peak near 57 ppm is the CH2 carbon attached to oxygen.

blocks.alt: 13C NMR spectrum on a ppm scale from 60 to 0: a green line near 57 ppm, a pink line near 18 ppm and a line labelled TMS at 0. Inset: the displayed formula HO-C-C-H of ethanol with the carbon next to OH in green and the other carbon in pink.
blocks.caption: Figure 30.7: 13C NMR spectrum of ethanol (printed as 'Figure 30.3'; original drawing after the textbook's figure).

blocks.text: 13C and 1H spectra differ in two key ways. In 13C NMR the relative peak area is usually not proportional to the number of carbon atoms, unlike 1H NMR, where the peak area shows the number of protons. The 13C peaks also do not show splitting, so they appear as single vertical lines. 13C NMR is less sensitive than 1H NMR.
